content.summary:
## Overview

This section separates three ideas the exam constantly mixes up: scalability (handling greater load by adapting), its two flavours (vertical = bigger instance, horizontal = more instances / elasticity), and high availability (surviving the loss of a data centre by running in at least two Availability Zones). Scalability is linked to but different from high availability. For EC2 the mapping is explicit: vertical = resize the instance (t2.nano up to u-12tb1.metal), horizontal = Auto Scaling Group plus Load Balancer (scale out / scale in), high availability = the same application across multiple AZs via ASG multi-AZ and Load Balancer multi-AZ.

## Core Concepts

- **Scalability:** An application or system can handle greater loads by adapting (scaling up/down or out/in).
- **Vertical scalability (scale up / down):** Increasing the size of the instance — e.g. moving an application from t2.micro to t2.large.
- **Horizontal scalability (elasticity, scale out / in):** Increasing the number of instances or systems for your application; implies distributed systems.
- **Distributed system:** An application spread over multiple instances/systems, which is what horizontal scaling requires and produces.
- **High availability:** Running your application/system in at least 2 data centers (== Availability Zones) so it can survive a data center loss.
- **Availability Zone (AZ):** A data center (as used in this section); high availability means spanning at least two of them.
- **Passive high availability:** Standby-style HA, e.g. RDS Multi AZ, where a second copy exists for failover rather than serving traffic.
- **Active high availability:** HA achieved by running the workload actively on several instances/AZs, as with horizontal scaling.
- **Auto Scaling Group (ASG):** The EC2 mechanism to increase/decrease the number of instances (scale out / scale in).
- **Load Balancer:** Distributes traffic across instances; multi-AZ placement makes it part of the HA design.
- **RDS Multi AZ:** The section's named example of passive high availability for a database.
- **ElastiCache / RDS vertical scaling:** Database/cache services that can be scaled vertically (increasing instance size).

## Key Comparisons

- **Vertical scalability vs Horizontal scalability:** Vertical changes the size of one instance (t2.micro → t2.large); horizontal changes the number of instances and therefore implies a distributed system.
- **Scalability vs High Availability:** Scalability handles greater load by adapting; high availability survives a data center loss by running in at least 2 AZs — linked but different goals.
- **Passive HA vs Active HA:** Passive keeps a standby (RDS Multi AZ); active runs the workload on multiple instances/ AZs (horizontal scaling).
- **Scale up/down vs Scale out/in:** Up/down = instance resizing (vertical); out/in = adding or removing instances via the Auto Scaling Group (horizontal).
- **ASG (horizontal) vs ASG multi AZ (HA):** An ASG alone changes instance count for load; spreading that ASG across AZs is what gives high availability.

## Common Misunderstandings

- Scaling vertically does not require a distributed system — it is the typical choice for non-distributed workloads such as a database.
- Horizontal scaling is not just 'more power': it implies a distributed architecture, which is why it suits web/modern applications.
- Scalability and high availability are not the same thing; being able to handle more load does not by itself mean you survive an AZ loss.
- High availability requires at least two Availability Zones, not merely more instances in the same one.
- Vertical scaling is not unlimited — there is usually a hardware ceiling.
- Adding an Auto Scaling Group does not by itself deliver HA unless it spans multiple AZs (and the load balancer does too).

## Mental Models

- Think of vertical scaling as promoting one call-centre operator to a more senior (bigger) one; horizontal scaling as hiring more operators.
- Think of HA as having a second building in another city so losing one building doesn't stop the business.
- Think of an ASG as a headcount dial and multi-AZ as where those heads sit.
- Think of RDS Multi AZ as a spare tire (passive) and horizontal scaling as a convoy of cars (active).

## Exceptions & Edge Cases

- Vertical scaling 'up' also has a 'down' direction (scale up / scale down) — resizing, not adding capacity.
- The t2.nano to u-12tb1.metal range is the source's stated span of EC2 instance sizes, not a per-family guarantee.
- Passive HA (RDS Multi AZ) is an example, not the only form of passive HA.
- Load balancer and ASG must both be multi-AZ for the full EC2 HA pattern as described.

## When to Use Which

- Workload is a non-distributed database needing more capacity → **Vertical scaling (e.g. resize RDS / ElastiCache instance)**
- Web/modern application must absorb variable traffic by adding instances → **Horizontal scaling with an Auto Scaling Group**
- Application must survive the loss of a data center → **Run across multiple AZs (ASG multi AZ + Load Balancer multi AZ)**
- Database needs standby-level resilience without app changes → **Passive HA such as RDS Multi AZ**
- Instance is simply undersized for one workload → **Vertical scaling: increase the instance size (scale up)**

## Patterns to Recognize

- 'increase the size of the instance' / t2.micro to t2.large → **Vertical scalability**
- 'increase the number of instances' / elasticity → **Horizontal scalability**
- 'survive a data center loss' / 'at least 2 Availability Zones' → **High availability**
- 'RDS Multi AZ' → **Passive high availability**
- 'scale out / scale in' → **Auto Scaling Group (horizontal scaling on EC2)**
- 'non-distributed system, such as a database' → **Vertical scaling**
- 'Load Balancer multi AZ' → **High availability on EC2**

## Exam Traps

- “'To handle more load, always scale vertically.'” — Vertical scaling hits a hardware limit and suits non-distributed systems; horizontal scaling is common for web/modern applications.
- “'High availability means running more instances.'” — HA specifically means running in at least two Availability Zones to survive a data center loss.
- “'Multi-AZ is the same as horizontal scaling.'” — HA goes hand in hand with horizontal scaling but is a distinct goal; passive HA (RDS Multi AZ) is not horizontal scaling.
- “'u-12tb1.metal is a database instance size cited by the section.'” — u-12tb1.metal (12.3 TB RAM, 448 vCPUs) is cited as the top of the EC2 vertical scaling range; RDS/ElastiCache are named as vertically scalable services.
- “'Scaling out and scaling up are synonyms.'” — Scale out/in = number of instances (ASG); scale up/down = instance size.

## Beyond the Source (tutor knowledge)

- Exam guide lists 'Horizontal scaling and vertical scaling' and 'Determining scaling strategies' under Design Resilient Architectures, and 'horizontal compared with vertical' scaling under cost-optimized compute — expect trade-off wording about cost and elasticity.
- Exam guide also emphasises mitigating single points of failure and failover strategies, so questions may combine multi-AZ with load balancing rather than testing definitions alone.

quiz.question: A team runs a small inventory application on a t2.micro instance. It needs more processing capacity, but the code is a single-tier monolith with no shared state layer. Which action best describes scaling this application vertically?
options: Add more t2.micro instances behind a Load Balancer and distribute traffic across them.
Resize the instance to a larger family, for example from t2.micro to t2.large.
Spread the existing t2.micro instance across two Availability Zones for resilience.
Place an Auto Scaling Group in front of the instance to add capacity on demand.
quiz.explanation: Vertical scaling means increasing the size of the instance, so moving from t2.micro to t2.large is the classic scale up. Adding instances behind a Load Balancer is horizontal scaling, not vertical. Spreading across two AZs is high availability, which does not increase per-instance capacity. An Auto Scaling Group changes instance count, which is horizontal, not vertical.

quiz.question: A startup expects sudden traffic spikes for a web application. It wants to add and remove compute capacity automatically as demand changes. Which property of horizontal scalability does this describe?
options: Elasticity: increase and decrease the number of instances to match load.
High availability: run the application in at least two Availability Zones.
Passive failover: keep a standby copy ready for failover.
Vertical scaling: replace the instance with a larger instance type.
quiz.explanation: Horizontal scalability is described in the source as elasticity, i.e. scaling out and in the number of instances. High availability is a different goal about surviving data-center loss across two AZs. Passive failover is a standby HA pattern such as RDS Multi AZ. Vertical scaling changes instance size, not instance count.

quiz.question: An application is being redesigned to run on many EC2 instances that share session state through a central store. Which architectural consequence should the team expect from adopting horizontal scaling?
options: The application becomes a distributed system and must tolerate partial failures.
The application can rely on one large instance and avoid coordinating nodes.
The application no longer needs a Load Balancer to route requests.
The application is guaranteed high availability without any AZ design.
quiz.explanation: Horizontal scaling implies distributed systems, so the application must be designed to coordinate across multiple systems. Relying on one large instance is vertical scaling, the opposite approach. A Load Balancer is still needed to distribute traffic. Horizontal scaling alone does not give high availability unless the instances are placed across multiple AZs.

quiz.question: A company must ensure its application survives the loss of a single AWS data center. What is the minimum requirement for high availability in this section?
options: Run the application in at least two Availability Zones.
Run the application on at least two instance sizes.
Run the application with an Auto Scaling Group in one AZ.
Run the application with a Load Balancer in one AZ.
quiz.explanation: High availability means running the application in at least two data centers, which are Availability Zones, so losing one does not stop the service. Using two instance sizes is vertical sizing, not HA. An ASG or Load Balancer inside a single AZ still fails if that AZ is lost.

quiz.question: A relational workload on Amazon RDS requires resilience against the failure of its Availability Zone but the application team cannot modify the application. Which design fits the section's example of passive high availability?
options: Deploy a database layer across several EC2 instances in multiple AZs and scale out.
Use Amazon RDS Multi AZ so a standby copy is available for failover.
Use an Auto Scaling Group to scale the database instances out and in.
Replace the database with a cache in a single AZ to reduce failure surface.
quiz.explanation: RDS Multi AZ is the section's named example of passive high availability, where a standby copy exists for failover without app changes. Running several EC2 database instances is active HA and would require application changes. An ASG is for EC2 horizontal scaling, not the managed database standby pattern. A single-AZ cache reduces resilience instead of improving it.

quiz.question: A web application runs several identical EC2 instances in multiple Availability Zones and all of them serve traffic simultaneously. Which type of high availability does this represent?
options: Passive high availability, because a standby is ready for failover.
Vertical high availability, because instance sizes are increased.
Active high availability, because the workload runs on multiple instances across AZs.
Elasticity, because instances are removed when traffic decreases.
quiz.explanation: Active high availability means the workload is actively served by several instances across AZs, as with horizontal scaling. Passive HA keeps a standby rather than serving traffic. Vertical scaling changes instance size and is not an HA type. Elasticity describes scaling out and in, not the HA posture itself.

quiz.question: A team already has an Auto Scaling Group and Load Balancer for a web tier. It must additionally survive the loss of one Availability Zone without changing the application. What should it do?
options: Increase the maximum instance size in the Auto Scaling Group launch configuration.
Move the Auto Scaling Group into a single AZ and increase desired capacity.
Keep the Load Balancer in one AZ and rely on the Auto Scaling Group for failover.
Configure the Auto Scaling Group and the Load Balancer to span multiple AZs.
quiz.explanation: For EC2, high availability is achieved by running the same application across multiple AZs through an ASG multi AZ and a Load Balancer multi AZ. Increasing instance size is vertical scaling and does not protect against AZ loss. Confining the ASG to one AZ reduces HA. A single-AZ Load Balancer remains a single point of failure.

quiz.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes scaling out from scaling up in the context of EC2?
options: Scaling out changes instance count via an ASG, while scaling up changes instance size.
Scaling out changes instance size, while scaling up changes instance count.
Scaling out adds AZs, while scaling up adds Load Balancers.
Scaling out and scaling up are both achieved by resizing the same instance.
quiz.explanation: Scale out and in refer to the number of instances and are handled by the Auto Scaling Group, while scale up and down refer to instance size. The reversed pairing is the trap. AZs are an HA concern, not what scaling out changes, and Load Balancers are added for traffic distribution. Scaling up does not add instances, so the two are not the same operation.
quiz.keyTopic: ASG scale out and scale in

quiz.question: An architect proposes handling all growth by vertically scaling a single EC2 instance from t2.nano up through larger families. Which constraint from the section makes this strategy unsuitable as the only long-term approach?
options: Vertical scaling is only possible for RDS and ElastiCache, not for EC2.
There is usually a hardware limit to how far an instance can be vertically scaled.
Vertical scaling requires a distributed system, which this design lacks.
Vertical scaling requires a Load Balancer, which single instances cannot use.
quiz.explanation: The source states there is usually a limit to how much you can vertically scale, a hardware ceiling, so it cannot absorb unlimited growth. Vertical scaling is available for EC2 as well as RDS and ElastiCache. It is the typical choice for non-distributed systems, so it does not require a distributed design. A Load Balancer is not a prerequisite for vertical scaling.

sections.title: Elastic Load Balancer Fundamentals: Purpose, Health Checks and Security Groups
sections.objective: Explain why a managed Elastic Load Balancer is used and how health checks and chained security groups keep traffic flowing only to healthy instances from the load balancer.
keyTopics: Load balancer single DNS access point
Health checks on port and route
Application security group restricting to LB
sections.text:
[Page 125]
What is load balancing?
Elastic Load Balancer EC2 Instance
EC2 Instance
EC2 Instance
• 	Load Balances are servers that forward traffic to multiple
servers (e.g., EC2 instances) downstream

[Page 126]
Why use a load balancer?
• 	Spread load across multiple downstream instances
• 	Expose a single point of access (DNS) to your application
• 	Seamlessly handle failures of downstream instances
• 	Do regular health checks to your instances
• 	Provide SSL termination (HTTPS) for your websites
• 	Enforce stickiness with cookies
• 	High availability across zones
• 	Separate public traffic from private traffic

[Page 127]
Why use an Elastic Load Balancer?
• 	An Elastic Load Balancer is a 	managed load balancer
• 	AWS guarantees that it will be working
• 	AWS takes care of upgrades, maintenance, high availability
• 	AWS provides only a few configuration knobs
• 	It costs less to setup your own load balancer but it will be a lot more effort
on your end
• 	It is integrated with many AWS offerings / services
• 	EC2, EC2 Auto Scaling Groups, Amazon ECS
• 	AWS Certificate Manager (ACM), CloudWatch
• 	Route 53, AWS WAF, AWS Global Accelerator

[Page 128]
Health Checks
• 	Health Checks are crucial for Load Balancers
• 	They enable the load balancer to know if instances it forwards traffic to
are available to reply to requests
• 	The health check is done on a port and a route (/health is common)
• 	If the response is not 200 (OK), then the instance is unhealthy
Elastic Load Balancer EC2 Instance
Health Checks
Protocol: HTTP
Port: 4567
Endpoint: /health

[Page 129]
Types of load balancer on AWS
• 	AWS has 4 kinds of managed Load Balancers
• 	Classic Load Balancer (v1 - old generation) – 2009 – CLB
• 	HTTP, HTTPS, TCP, SSL (secure TCP)
• 	Application Load Balancer (v2 - new generation) – 2016 – ALB
• 	HTTP, HTTPS, WebSocket
• 	Network Load Balancer (v2 - new generation) – 2017 – NLB
• 	TCP, TLS (secure TCP), UDP
• 	Gateway Load Balancer – 2020 – GWLB
• 	Operates at layer 3 (Network layer) – IP Protocol
• 	Overall, it is recommended to use the newer generation load balancers as they
provide more features
• 	Some load balancers can be setup as internal (private) or external (public) ELBs

sections.title: Sticky Sessions, Cross-Zone Load Balancing and SSL/TLS Certificates
sections.objective: Apply stickiness, cross-zone load balancing and SNI-based multi-certificate HTTPS configurations, and identify which ELB types support each feature and where extra costs apply.
keyTopics: Cross-zone load balancing default per ELB
sections.text:
[Page 143]
Sticky Sessions (Session Affinity)
• 	It is possible to implement stickiness so that the
same client is always redirected to the same
instance behind a load balancer
• 	This works for Classic Load Balancer, Application
Load Balancer, and Network Load Balancer
• 	For both CLB & ALB, the “cookie” used for
stickiness has an expiration date you control
• 	Use case: make sure the user doesn’t lose his
session data
• 	Enabling stickiness may bring imbalance to the
load over the backend EC2 instances

• 	Application-based 	Cookies

• 	Can include any custom attributes required by the application
• 	Cookie name must be specified individually for each target group
• 	Don’t use AWSALB, AWSALBAPP, or AWSALBTG (reserved for use by the ELB)
• 	Application cookie
• 	Generated by the load balancer
• 	Cookie name is AWSALBAPP
• 	Duration-based 	Cookies
• 	Cookie generated by the load balancer
• 	Cookie name is AWSALB for ALB, AWSELB for CLB

[Page 147]
SSL/TLS 	- 	Basics
• 	An SSL Certificate allows traffic between your clients and your load balancer
to be encrypted in transit (in-flight encryption)
• 	SSL refers to Secure Sockets Layer, used to encrypt connections
• 	TLS refers to Transport Layer Security, which is a newer version
• 	Nowadays, TLS certificates are mainly used, but people still refer as SSL
• 	Public SSL certificates are issued by Certificate Authorities (CA)
• 	Comodo, Symantec, GoDaddy, GlobalSign, Digicert, Letsencrypt, etc…
• 	SSL certificates have an expiration date (you set) and must be renewed

[Page 148]
Load Balancer 	- 	SSL Certificates
• 	The load balancer uses an X.509 certificate (SSL/TLS server certificate)
• 	You can manage certificates using ACM (AWS Certificate Manager)
• 	You can create upload your own certificates alternatively
• 	HTTPS listener:
• 	You must specify a default certificate
• 	You can add an optional list of certs to support multiple domains
• 	Clients can use SNI (Server Name Indication) to specify the hostname they reach
• 	Ability to specify a security policy to support older versions of SSL / TLS (legacy clients)

Connection Draining
• 	Feature naming
• 	Connection Draining – for CLB
• 	Deregistration Delay – for ALB & NLB
• 	Time to complete “in-flight requests” while the
instance is de-registering or unhealthy
• 	Stops sending new requests to the EC2
instance which is de-registering
• 	Between 1 to 3600 seconds (default: 300
seconds)
• 	Can be disabled (set value to 0)
• 	Set to a low value if your requests are short

[Page 152]
What’s an Auto Scaling Group?
• 	In real-life, the load on your websites and application can change
• 	In the cloud, you can create and get rid of servers very quickly
• 	The goal of an Auto Scaling Group (ASG) is to:
• 	Scale out (add EC2 instances) to match an increased load
• 	Scale in (remove EC2 instances) to match a decreased load
• 	Ensure we have a minimum and a maximum number of EC2 instances running
• 	Automatically register new instances to a load balancer
• 	Re-create an EC2 instance in case a previous one is terminated (ex: if unhealthy)
• 	ASG are free (you only pay for the underlying EC2 instances)

sections.title: Auto Scaling Policies, Metrics and Cooldowns
sections.objective: Select the right scaling policy and metric for a workload scenario, and explain how cooldown periods and AMI readiness affect how quickly an ASG stabilizes.
sections.text:
[Page 157]
Auto Scaling Groups 	– 	Scaling Policies
• 	Dynamic Scaling
• 	Target Tracking Scaling
• 	Simple to set-up
• 	Example: I want the average ASG CPU to stay at around 40%
• 	Simple / Step Scaling
• 	When a CloudWatch alarm is triggered (example CPU > 70%), then add 2 units
• 	When a CloudWatch alarm is triggered (example CPU < 30%), then remove 1
• 	Scheduled Scaling
• 	Anticipate a scaling based on known usage patterns
• 	Example: increase the min capacity to 10 at 5 pm on Fridays

[Page 158]
Auto Scaling Groups 	– 	Scaling Policies
• 	Predictive scaling: 	continuously forecast load and schedule scaling ahead

[Page 159]

across your instances
• 	RequestCountPerTarget: to make sure
the number of requests per EC2
instances is stable
• 	Average Network In / Out 	(if you’re
application is network bound)
• 	Any custom metric 	(that you push
using CloudWatch)
